archetype.name: Dual-Threat (scramble-first)
archetype.definition: An accurate, aggressive downfield passer whose rushing value comes almost entirely from breaking the pocket on dropbacks, not from designed runs.

report.headline: Slow start against top defenses is over; the turnovers are the remaining tax.
report.take:
Maye is coming off a 2025 that ranked third in the league in EPA per play, completion over expected and yards per attempt. His 2026 line looks like a step back: 0.126 EPA per dropback, 17th of 43 qualifiers, with 7 interceptions, the second-most at the position. Most of that drop is front-loaded and tied to his opponents. Three of his first five games came against defenses now ranked 2nd (SEA) and 3rd (JAX), plus a Pittsburgh game where he was pressured on 37% of dropbacks. His pass EPA in those three games was -4.6, -1.3 and -14.2. Against Buffalo and Las Vegas it was +11 and +29.5. The accuracy never went away: his CPOE of 6.18 ranks 5th, and his bad-throw rate of 8.6% ranks 8th of 36.

The profile hasn't changed. He still pushes the ball and is still very good at it. His 23 throws of 20+ air yards are worth 0.804 EPA each, and the intermediate band adds 0.384. When the pocket breaks, his 17 scrambles have produced 162 yards and 11 first downs at nearly a full point of EPA per scramble. That scrambling is why his rushing yards rank 5th even though his six designed runs have netted 1.33 yards a carry. His 3.06-second time to throw is the cost of extending plays, and this year he is paying less for it. His pressure-to-sack rate fell to 27.8%, down from 40.5% as a rookie and 35.6% last year.

The numbers hide two things. The first is that the offense's floor is being dragged down by the easy stuff. Throws behind the line (-0.366 EPA on 31 attempts), under-center dropbacks (-0.379) and targets to Rhamondre Stevenson (-0.166 per target) are all losing plays. That is a scheme and personnel problem more than a quarterback one. The second is that the interception count overstates the decision-making but doesn't invent it. He has 7 picks plus 5 turnover-worthy fumbles, and three interceptions came in close fourth quarters. He threw 10 as a rookie and 8 last year, so some risk-taking is who he is. The current 4.6% pick rate, though, is well above last season's pace and should come down.

From here, expect something closer to the late-September-onward version than the opening three weeks. The schedule softened, the downfield game is landing, and the sack avoidance looks like real growth in year three. It probably won't be the full 2025 peak. A.J. Brown is on IR after playing one game, the run game ranks 23rd in EPA, and third down (-0.119 EPA) and the red zone (-0.064) still stall.

strengths.title: Downfield and intermediate accuracy
strengths.body: His deep throws are producing 0.804 EPA per attempt with a 12.8 CPOE. The 10-19 yard band adds 0.384, so the vertical game is carrying the offense. This matches his 2025 profile, when he ranked third in CPOE, so it should last, even if the deep EPA cools from a 23-attempt sample.

strengths.title: Scrambles that move the chains
strengths.body: He scrambles on 9.4% of dropbacks. Eleven of his 17 scrambles went for first downs, at 0.956 EPA each, which more than pays for the long time to throw. It has been a trait across all three seasons, with top-10 rushing yardage each year, so it is a stable part of his value.

strengths.title: Sack avoidance has improved
strengths.body: His pressure-to-sack rate is 27.8%, down from 40.5% as a rookie and 35.6% in 2025, even while holding the ball over three seconds. That reads as real growth in how he escapes and finds outlets rather than luck. It should mostly hold, though it gets tested this week.

concerns.title: Turnovers, especially late and close
concerns.body: He has 7 interceptions (42nd of 43) and 5 turnover-worthy fumbles. Three of the picks came in one-score fourth quarters, where his EPA is -0.098. Some of this is the price of a vertical, extend-the-play style, and his career pick totals say it won't vanish. But a bad-throw rate ranked 8th suggests the 4.6% interception rate should drift down.

concerns.title: Dead weight in the short game
concerns.body: Throws behind the line of scrimmage lose 0.366 EPA each. Under-center dropbacks are worse at -0.379, and Stevenson's 20 targets are a net negative. That is the scheme and personnel bleeding value on supposedly safe plays. It is fixable with play-calling but has persisted for five games.

concerns.title: Third down and red zone stall
concerns.body: He converts 36.4% on third down with an average of 7 yards to go, at -0.119 EPA. Red-zone dropbacks are slightly negative. Both are small samples (44 and 27 plays) and were strong areas in his 2025 season, so this is more likely to improve than define him.

trend.note: His pass EPA was negative in each of the first three games, against two top-3 defenses and a heavy-pressure Pittsburgh front, then went +11 at Buffalo and +29.5 against Las Vegas. He has covered in each of the last three.

nextGame.headline: Big favorite, but the Jets' pass rush tests his weakest link
nextGame.body:
The Jets are an uneven defense, and the uneven parts point at Maye. They are 18th in pass EPA allowed and middle-of-the-pack deep, which suits his vertical game. But they rank 2nd in sack rate and 7th against the run, and they have held quarterbacks to 209 passing yards a game, the 3rd-fewest. They have been stingiest of all against tight ends (-0.31 EPA per target, 1st) and have held opposing WR1s and WR2s well under their averages. Their soft spot is the third receiver (0.64 EPA per target, 29th). In an offense where Mack Hollins (0.636 per target) and DeMario Douglas (0.581) have been his most efficient options, that is a lane he can use. With New England's run game ranked 23rd against a strong Jets run defense, expect another pass-heavy script.

Availability cuts both ways. Left tackle Will Campbell, an 87%-snap starter, is questionable with a knee sprain right before a top-2 pass rush. If he sits, the sack and hit numbers likely climb. The Jets lose a little of their own rush: Braiden McGregor is on IR and Joseph Ossai is questionable, though both are part-timers. A.J. Brown has only a chance to return to practice, and TreVeyon Henderson is questionable. The bigger news is the Jets' offense, which is already 20th in EPA and is missing Breece Hall, Adonai Mitchell and guard Dylan Parham. That should hand New England favorable field position and a lead to protect.

keyMatchups.title: Jets pass rush vs. Campbell's knee
keyMatchups.body: New York sacks quarterbacks on 9.1% of dropbacks, 2nd in the league, and Maye holds the ball 3.06 seconds. His improved escapability has kept sacks down. Without his starting left tackle, that improvement faces its hardest test of the year.

keyMatchups.title: Third receiver against a weak spot
keyMatchups.body: The Jets have been gashed by WR3s at 0.64 EPA per target, while their tight end coverage is the league's best. Getting the ball to Hollins or Douglas rather than forcing it to Hunter Henry is the efficient route.

keyMatchups.title: Depleted Jets offense shapes script
keyMatchups.body: The Jets' offense is 20th in EPA before losing Hall, Mitchell and Parham. New England's pass defense ranks 5th. A comfortable lead lowers Maye's volume, but he has been sharp when leading by 9+, at 0.391 EPA.

nextGame.watch: Whether Campbell plays, and how Maye's pressure-to-sack rate holds up against the league's second-best sack unit.

restOfSeason.body:
The accuracy, the deep game and the scrambling are all multi-season traits, so the efficiency should settle in the top-12 range rather than the 17th he sits at now. The interception rate is the clearest regression candidate. At a career-like pace he would throw closer to one every other game than the 1.4 a game he has averaged so far. The deep-ball EPA will also cool from a 23-attempt sample.

What keeps him short of his 2025 level is the supporting cast. A 23rd-ranked run game puts more on his arm on third down, Brown has played one game, and the screen and under-center game keeps costing value. A Brown return and a cleaner short game are what would push him back toward elite efficiency.
swingFactors: Campbell's knee and the pass protection

bets.reason: The Jets allow the 3rd-fewest passing yards to quarterbacks (209 a game) and have the 2nd-best sack rate, and his left tackle is questionable. A depleted Jets offense also points to a New England lead and a lighter fourth quarter.

The Jets' offense is 20th in EPA and now lacks Hall, Mitchell and Parham against New England's 5th-ranked pass defense. The Jets' run defense (7th) and pass rush also slow a Patriots offense whose ground game ranks 23rd. Three of New England's five games went under.

He has thrown a pick in four of five games and has always carried an interception habit (10 and 8 in his first two seasons). The Jets' pressure tends to force rushed throws, even if his rate should cool.
He holds the ball over three seconds against the league's 2nd-best sack-rate defense, possibly without his 87%-snap left tackle.

confidence.note: Five games, split between top-3 and bottom-tier defenses. Two strong seasons of career context help, but Brown's and Campbell's statuses are open questions.
